title: The 10-Minute Account Safety Reset
dek: If you only have time to secure one account today, start with the email account that resets the others.
description: A prioritized ten-minute account security checklist covering email, passkeys or MFA, recovery details, sessions, and software updates.
takeaway: Secure your primary email first because it often receives password-reset links for other accounts.
Use a passkey when the service and your recovery setup support it; otherwise use a unique managed password plus MFA.
Check recovery details and active sessions, then install pending security updates.

sections.heading: Why email comes first
paragraphs: Your main email account is often the recovery route for shopping, social, work, and financial services. Someone who controls that inbox may be able to request reset links for other accounts, read security alerts, and hide evidence by deleting or forwarding messages.

That makes email a useful first target for a short security reset. This checklist is for preventive maintenance. If you already see an unknown login, a password change you did not make, or messages you did not send, use the provider's account-recovery process immediately instead.

sections.heading: Minutes 0–3: strengthen the sign-in
paragraphs: Open the email provider through its official app or a known address. In its security settings, create a passkey if you understand where it will be stored and how you would recover access. If a passkey is not available or is not right for your devices, use a long, unique password generated by a reputable password manager.

Turn on multifactor authentication. Prefer a phishing-resistant option such as a passkey or security key when available. An authenticator app is generally a stronger fallback than a text code, but any supported MFA is better than relying on a password alone.

sections.heading: Minutes 3–6: check recovery and sessions
paragraphs: Review the recovery phone numbers and email addresses. Remove anything you do not recognize or can no longer access. If the provider offers backup or recovery codes, generate a current set and store it somewhere you can reach if the phone is lost—not only on that phone.

Open the list of signed-in devices or recent security activity. Sign out sessions you do not recognize. If the service offers a single 'sign out everywhere' control and you suspect compromise, use it after changing the sign-in method.

sections.heading: Minutes 6–8: look for hidden changes
paragraphs: Check email forwarding, filters, delegates, and connected applications. An unwanted forwarding rule can quietly copy messages even after a password change. Remove rules, app access, or delegates you did not create.
Scan the sent and deleted folders for activity you do not recognize. This does not prove the account is clean, but it can reveal that someone used it and help you tell contacts what happened.

sections.heading: Minutes 8–10: update the device and choose the next account
paragraphs: Install pending security updates for the device, browser, and email app. Updates repair known flaws; delaying them can leave an otherwise strong account exposed through the software used to reach it.

Then schedule the next account rather than trying to fix everything at once. A good order is password manager, financial accounts, mobile carrier, cloud storage, and social accounts. Reuse the same process, but never reuse the same password.
steps: Secure primary email with a passkey or a unique managed password.
Turn on the strongest MFA option you can reliably recover.
Verify recovery contacts and store new backup codes safely.
Review devices, sessions, forwarding rules, and connected apps.
Install updates and put the next important account on your calendar.
